title: Can you trust this announcement?
objective: Check three claims in an AI-written message against the original notice and show your evidence.
example: An AI says the library opens at eight. I check the hours posted by the librarian before telling a friend when to meet.

terms.meaning: A kind of AI trained on examples of language. It uses learned patterns to predict the next small piece of text in a response.
A statement that you can check against evidence.

caseText: Finish the line “At twilight, the astronomy club looked up and saw ___.” Several endings would sound right. Which one actually happened? Now edit a pretend AI draft for the club. Families will use it to decide when to arrive and what to bring.
evidence: A. Original notice, signed by the science teacher on October 2. “Sky Watch meets October 9, 6–7 p.m., on the east field. Borrow a star chart at the door.”
B. Sample AI draft, October 3. “Sky Watch starts at 6 p.m. on October 9 in the west field. A free telescope will be waiting for every visitor.”
tasks: Make three rows on paper for the start date and time, the location, and the telescope promise. For each, mark supported, contradicted, or still unknown. Quote the words from A that led you there, or name what A leaves out.
Rewrite B in two sentences a family could use. Underline each detail you kept and point to the matching words in A.
Write the question you would ask the science teacher before adding the telescope claim. Explain why getting another convincing answer from the same AI would leave the question open.
exit: A new draft says visitors can borrow star charts. Which words support it? Which claim from the first draft still needs a person to confirm it?

teacher.instruction: Collect three plausible endings to the twilight sentence. Ask what a witness would need to tell us to establish which one happened.
Explain how predicting pieces of text can produce a convincing sentence with a wrong detail. Invite students to choose one claim and point to the record they would use to check it.
Pairs classify the three claims. Ask them to justify each label with the original notice, including how they handled any detail that was hard to check.
Trade rewritten announcements. Have the other pair trace every published detail to the signed notice.
Collect the exit response and look for the difference between a contradiction and an unanswered question.

lookFor: The editor gives a reason for each claim label, traces the revised announcement to specific words in the source, and identifies an appropriate way to resolve an open question.
support: Fold a page in half. Put the AI's words on the left and the teacher's exact words on the right. Use a question mark when the notice is silent.
stretch: Could the newer date on B settle the location? Explain what would give a later update authority to change it.

title: Whose vote is missing?
objective: Use survey counts to find a missing perspective in an AI recommendation and design a fairer next step.
example: I ask only the orchestra what music to play at lunch. Before I call their pick the school's favorite, I want to hear from students outside orchestra.

terms.meaning: The group you collect information from.
A pattern that can give some people or outcomes an unfair advantage. How people collect and use data can introduce bias.

caseText: Cedar Middle wants a meeting time that works for as many students as possible. An editor gave an AI tool the first survey and asked it to recommend a time. The principal is waiting for your review.
evidence: A. The PE teacher asked 12 students at early practice. Ten picked before school and two picked lunch. Students had to choose one.
B. Sample AI recommendation. “Most Cedar Middle students prefer before school. Move all club meetings to 7:30 a.m.”
C. A counselor later asked 12 different students getting off the last morning bus. Two picked before school and ten picked lunch. The bus arrives at 7:50 a.m.
tasks: Draw a tally table with one row for each survey and columns for before school and lunch. Add a totals row. Describe who the first survey could reach and who it might miss.
Read B aloud. Cross out any words the first survey cannot support. Explain what changes when you add C and what you still cannot conclude about the whole school.
Write a two-sentence note to the principal. Name another way to collect voices, one group it would reach, and the person who should hear from students before setting the time.
exit: Finish this thought with numbers from the case. “I would pause the 7:30 decision because ___. Before choosing a time, I would ___.”

teacher.instruction: Read only A and B at first. Ask students which words in B make a claim about people who were never asked.
Introduce sample and bias. Sketch the first tally row and identify how the place and time shaped the sample.
Reveal C. Let pairs combine the counts, check the totals, and discuss which students would have trouble attending at 7:30.
Swap notes to the principal. Ask each reader to name one group the proposed follow-up would actually reach.
Collect the exit response. Ask students which conclusion their numbers support and whose views still need to be heard.

lookFor: Students show how they combined both sets of counts. Their note connects the sampling method to a group it may miss and proposes a workable way to include those students before a person decides.
support: Use 12 counters for each survey. Move each counter under a time label and record how many are in each pile.
stretch: The survey offered two times. Propose a question that lets someone explain why neither time works. Who should hear those answers?

title: Who said we could use that?
objective: Choose media that fits its permission, credit the creator, and explain how AI helped with an edit.
example: Nia lets me play her song on our class podcast if I credit her. My closing line says, “Music by Nia. AI helped me shorten the introduction.”

terms.meaning: A person's freely given agreement to a particular use, audience, or action.
Naming the creator the way they asked.
Telling the audience what help a person or tool provided.

caseText: The Make & Mend Club needs a printed poster for its classroom door. The team has a photo, a drawing, and a caption from a pretend AI editing session. Decide what can go on the door.
evidence: A. The photographer says the repair-table photo may appear in the closed class slideshow. The two students pictured agreed to the slideshow. No one has agreed to a hallway display or an upload to an AI tool.
B. Kai drew a wrench. Kai's note says, “Use my wrench drawing on the classroom-door poster and in the school bulletin. Credit me as K. Keep the drawing as it is.”

C. The editor asked for headline ideas using only the words “school repair club.” The sample AI suggested “Give it a second life.” The club has approved a headline brainstorm. Its teacher will review the final poster.
tasks: For A and B, list the allowed audience and use. Pick a visual for the classroom door, or design a text-only poster. Explain the permission behind your choice.

Sketch the poster on paper. If you use the wrench, label a box for Kai's original drawing and write the requested credit. If you borrow the AI headline, add a short note explaining the AI's help and the human editor's work.
Your partner wants to send the photo to an AI editor to remove the background. Write a reply that protects the people pictured and gives the team a usable alternative.
exit: Someone writes “Photo by our club” under the photo. Which permissions would the team still need before publishing it on the door?

teacher.instruction: Compare the audiences of a closed slideshow, a classroom door, and a school bulletin. Ask who can see each one.
Read the permission cards. Make separate marks for who created an item, who appears in it, and where it may be shared.
Pairs sketch the poster and add any needed credit and disclosure. Ask them to justify each item they choose.
Partners trade posters and act as editors. Ask them to point to a permission for each visual and account for any AI-written words.
Collect the exit response and ask each student to distinguish the creator's role from the role of the people appearing in a picture.

lookFor: Students tie their media decision to the stated audience and permission. Their poster credits the work it uses, accounts for any AI contribution, and identifies who reviewed the finished work.
support: Write three labels beside each item on paper. Use creator, allowed audience, and credit. Read the matching words in the evidence aloud.
stretch: The school wants to publish the same poster on its public website. Identify exactly which part of Kai's permission would need a new conversation.

title: Draft a Safe-to-Share bulletin
objective: Prepare a club bulletin with checked event details and a private editor's note explaining your security and AI decisions.
example: An AI draft of a team flyer lists a player's phone number. I leave the number out and check the game time with the coach before sharing the flyer.

terms.meaning: Checking a claim with an original record or with someone who can confirm it through a known school channel.
A short account of something concerning, sent to someone who can help.

caseText: You edit Cedar Middle's club bulletin. Other students want to come to a repair café, where people learn how to fix everyday things. A draft, a chat message, and the advisor's records disagree. Work only with the fictional records below.
evidence: A. November 12 notice from the advisor, on the school club board. “Make & Mend repair café, November 20, 3:15–4:00 p.m., Room 204. Free. Sign up in class. Bring your questions.”
B. Sample AI draft. “Give it a second life! The repair café starts at 3 p.m. in Room 240. Reserve your free seat online.” The draft supplies no source.

C. November 13 message from an unknown account. “To reserve your place, send me your school password and a photo.” The advisor confirmed in class that no password, outside form, or photo is part of signup. The advisor handles suspicious club messages in person.

D. Media permission. Kai allows the original wrench drawing in the school bulletin with credit to K. The group photo was approved only for a closed class slideshow. Your editor may use an AI headline idea if the bulletin explains its use.
tasks: Draw a line down your paper. Use one side for a public bulletin and the other for a private editor's note. In the bulletin, include the event, date, time, room, cost, and how to join. Choose a permitted visual or use text only.

In your editor's note, trace two event details to a dated record. Explain one AI detail you corrected. If you borrow a headline, disclose the help in the bulletin. If you write your own, record that choice in the note. Explain your choice of visual and include any needed credit.

Write a two-sentence practice report to the advisor on the private side. Describe the unexpected request and its date, how you checked the real signup, and what help you want. Keep private information out of both pieces. Save your draft on paper for the next lesson.
exit: Circle one change that protects another student. Underline one change that makes your bulletin more accurate. Explain both to a partner.

teacher.instruction: Assign the role of bulletin editor. Set up two paper sections and decide who needs to read each one.
Model tracing one fact to the advisor's notice. Ask pairs to identify which document can establish the signup process.
Students draft their bulletin and private note, independently or with a partner. Prompt for time, room, source, media, AI use, and report recipient.
A second editor checks one event detail and one privacy choice. Return the draft to its author for a first revision.
Hear the exit explanations. Keep each draft and note together for the next class.

lookFor: Another reader could attend using the bulletin and trace its details to a dated record. The editor accounts for any artwork or AI wording. The private report describes the concern, identifies where to send it, and shares only the details needed for help.
support: Try these lines. “Join us on ___ in ___. Sign up ___.” “I checked ___ against ___.” “I am reporting ___ because ___.”
stretch: A classmate wants to put the whole suspicious message on the public bulletin. Suggest a short, useful signup reminder and explain what belongs only in the advisor's report.

title: Audit and revise the bulletin
objective: Decide which new information changes the bulletin, then document a correction another editor can verify.
example: Yesterday I told the team to wear blue. After the coach confirms a switch to white, I post a correction where the team read the first message.

terms.meaning: A careful check of a piece of work against its evidence and requirements.
A notice that tells readers what changed and what to do with the updated information.

caseTitle: A room change and a rumor
caseText: It is November 19. The club's first bulletin is already on the school club board. Review a partner's draft as a second editor. If you need a starting copy, use the backup bulletin in A. Work on paper and simulate posting the correction.
evidence: A. Backup bulletin based on the advisor's November 12 notice. “Make & Mend repair café, November 20, 3:15–4:00 p.m., Room 204. Free. Sign up in class.”

B. November 18 update in the school office notices. The club advisor confirmed it in person. “The repair café will meet in the library from 3:30–4:00 p.m. on November 20. All other details are the same.”
C. November 19 anonymous chat. “Heard it's canceled. Pass it on.” The message does not name a source. The advisor can be reached in class.

D. The advisor's signup is in class. An unknown account requested passwords and photos on November 13. The advisor takes reports in person and requires neither for signup. Kai permits the unchanged wrench drawing in the bulletin with credit to K. The group photo is for the closed class slideshow only. Disclose any AI headline used.
tasks: Audit the first bulletin. Alongside each event detail, mark keep, change, or check and name the source. Write one question about the cancellation rumor and name a known school channel where an editor could ask it.

Revise the bulletin and write a one-sentence correction for the same club board its readers used. Show exactly which time and place changed. Check signup, media permission, credit, and AI disclosure before you hand it back.

Finish a change log with three entries. For each, name the old detail or concern, your decision, and the record that supports it. Include your decision about the rumor. If starting from A, add a private note on the password request and whether you used AI wording.

Exchange or reread your work. Check whether a reader knows where and when to show up, how to join safely, and which changes came from a confirmed source. Initial the paper as editor using a fictional initial.
exit: The anonymous chat has the newest date. Why did you use B to revise the bulletin? What would you do if the advisor later confirmed the cancellation?

teacher.instruction: Return prior drafts and supply A for anyone who needs it. Introduce the office update and the newer chat message together.
Partners label details keep, change, or check. Ask how an editor knows who issued each message.
Students revise the bulletin, write a correction for its original audience, and complete the change log.
Exchange work for a final audit. Check event details, signup and reporting decisions, media and AI choices, and how the editor handled conflicting reports.
Collect the revised bulletin, editor's note, and change log. Have each student explain what future evidence could change their decision.

lookFor: The correction tells earlier readers exactly what changed and where to find current information. The editor traces the revisions to a source, explains how they weighed conflicting messages, and documents their decisions for a second reader.
support: Use a three-column change log. Head the columns “What I read,” “What I changed or kept,” and “How I know.” A partner can record your spoken explanation.
stretch: One old copy is still on a second bulletin board. Draft the message that lets those readers find the correction and explain how you would check it reached them.
